docs.text: MotorMovementData A NumPy array with named dimensions, labels and metadata. print ( data ) # nice summary: metric, shape, dimensions + labels, NaN %, layout data . dimensions # ('participants', 'repetitions', 'images', 'targets', 'timepoints') data . describe_dimensions () # axis, length and labels per dimension data . axes # current axis of each dimension, e.g. {'participants': 0, ...} data . axis_of ( "repetitions" ) # axis of one dimension (updated after select / average) data . images # or data["images"]: image of each entry on the images axis data . targets # or data["targets"]: response buttons, in the order of the data data . participants , data . repetitions , data . timepoints # same for the other dimensions data [ "coordinates" ] # x/y labels (data.coordinates is the dict of all labels) data . metric # 'euclidean', 'cosine' or 'position' data . trial_info ( participants = 1 , images = "image_1" ) # button + start positions of those trials Metadata Where distance type data.metric image IDs data.images , data.coordinates["images"] response / start button positions data.trial_info(...) , data.metadata["button_positions"] meaning of each dimension data.dimensions , data.axes , data.describe_dimensions() targets (response buttons) data.targets time unit and step data.metadata["time_unit"] , ["sampling_interval"] Methods data.average("repetitions") or data.average(["participants", "repetitions"]) : NaN-aware mean over named dimensions (or axes). data.select(participants=2) or data.select(images=["b", "a"], repetitions=1) : select by label. A single label removes that dimension; a list keeps it, in the order given. Singular names work ( participant=2 ). data.downsample(250) : keep every n-th time point to reach about 250 Hz. data.save("file.npz", downsample_hz=None) : compressed .npz (no pickle). downsample_hz=250 or 500 downsamples first; the object is untouched. MotorMovementData.load("file.npz") . Dimensions move when you select or average select with a single label and average remove a dimension, so the remaining ones are renumbered. data.axes and data.axis_of(name) always describe the current array. Asking for the labels of a removed dimension (e.g. one.participants after select(participants=2) ) raises an error that says how it was removed.

docs.text: Distances extract_distance(preprocessed_df, metric="euclidean", target_names=None, position_col=None, duration=None, sampling_interval=1.0, fill_start=False, progress=True) returns a MotorMovementData . Metrics metric Value Dimensions "euclidean" distance to each response button (standardised space) participants, repetitions, images, targets, timepoints "cosine" cosine distance between movement direction (from the start button) and each button direction same "position" x and y positions by default; set position_col="x_std" or "y_std" to return only one column participants, repetitions, images, coordinates, timepoints by default; no targets The repetitions dimension is always kept, also with a single repetition. For the default position output, coordinates has labels ["x_std", "y_std"] . Target order Button names and positions come from the preprocessed dataframe. target_names sets the order of the targets dimension, as names (ignoring case, spaces and punctuation) or indices. Default: the order found in the data. Time axis and interpolation Mouse samples are irregular (about every 16 ms). Per trial, x and y are linearly interpolated onto a regular grid ( time column, ms), then the distances are computed. duration : length of the array in ms (e.g. 1000 ). Default: the latest time point in the whole dataset. sampling_interval : grid step in ms. Default 1 (one entry per ms). Use e.g. 4 for 250 Hz to get smaller arrays. Before a trial's first sample the position is unknown: the array is NaN there. fill_start=True instead assumes the cursor was at the start-button centre at time 0 and interpolates up to the first sample. After the trial's last sample (trial ended) the array is always NaN. The timepoints coordinate holds the grid times in ms. Progress bar A tqdm progress bar over trials is shown by default ( progress=False hides it). preprocess_mouse_tracking_data has the same option.
docs.title: Distances

docs.text: Input data One row per trial; one dataframe (CSV) per participant. Mouse samples live in a mouse_tracking_data column as a list (or JSON string) of {"x": ..., "y": ..., "t": <ms>, "event": ...} . Required columns Standard name Meaning response response given (used to detect completed trials) accuracy correct / incorrect stimulus image shown (a path or html containing it) mouse_tracking_data the samples described above response_button_names list of button labels screen_width , screen_height window size in px response_button_positions one rectangle per button starting_button_position rectangle of the start button trial_type and event are optional and not used by the pipeline; they are handy to write a row_mask (e.g. to leave out training trials). A rectangle is (bottom-left x, bottom-left y, width, height) in pixels, origin at the top left of the window (so "bottom" is the larger y). If your columns are named differently, check_columns detects common aliases or accepts a mapping, and raises an error listing what is missing: check_columns ( df , column_map = { "accuracy" : "correct" }) preprocess_mouse_tracking_data ( df , column_map = { "accuracy" : "correct" }) Output columns All your columns are kept. Added or filled in (standard names, only where the source information exists): ppt_number , repetition , stimulus (image ID), response_button_names , starting_button_position , starting_button_position_std , response_button_positions , response_button_positions_std , time , x_std , y_std , std_scale , plus a standard-named copy of any mapped column ( response , accuracy , ...).

docs.text: Plotting Both functions take a preprocessed dataframe (one or many trials) and return a matplotlib Axes ; call plt.show() yourself. ax = plot_trials ( pre , color_by = "accuracy" , palette = { 0 : "salmon" , 1 : "teal" }, excluded_indices = excluded_idx , button_shape = "circle" ) Argument Meaning color_by , palette column used for colours and optional {value: colour} excluded_indices these rows are drawn gray and labelled "excluded" button_shape , start_shape "rectangle" (default) or "circle" (an oval inscribed in the button rectangle if width != height) show_buttons draw start/response buttons in gray in the background invert_yaxis , alpha , ax axis orientation, line transparency, axes to draw on plot_trials keeps each trial's own screen coordinates (any number of buttons). plot_binary_trials is for two-button tasks: it mirrors trials left-right so the buttons line up with the first trial's order, or with response_button_order=["inanimate", "animate"] .

docs.text: Preprocessing and exclusions preprocess_mouse_tracking_data(df_or_list, ...) Hands-off: all rows and all columns are kept . The output is your dataframe plus the columns computed here; only the rows that can be processed get them filled in, the others (surveys, instructions, rows without a trajectory) keep empty values. processed_trial_mask(df) tells which rows were processed. check_columns finds the columns holding the needed information. Where your column has another name, a copy is added under the standard name (yours is kept; column_map={"accuracy": "correct"} says where things are). A row is processed when it has mouse samples, a stimulus, button names, a valid screen size and parsable button positions. Rows with samples that fail one of these are reported in a warning. row_mask restricts the rows further, e.g. row_mask=lambda d: ~d["event"].fillna("").str.contains("training") to leave out training trials (they are processed by default). Processed rows get: stimulus as image ID, parsed button names and positions, time , x_std , y_std , starting_button_position_std , response_button_positions_std , repetition (if absent), std_scale . Given a list of dataframes it concatenates them and adds ppt_number (1, 2, ...). A tqdm progress bar is shown (per row, or per participant for a list); pass progress=False to hide it. Standardised coordinates The origin is the screen centre. With scaling="min_side" (default) both axes are divided by half the shorter screen side , so distances and angles keep their true proportions: buttons placed on a circle around the start button stay equidistant from it, and x_std spans [-width/height, width/height] on a landscape screen while y_std spans [-1, 1] . scaling="stretch" instead maps both axes to [-1, 1] , which squeezes the longer side (fine for two buttons on a horizontal line, wrong for circular layouts). invert_y=True (default) makes up positive. std_scale holds the pixels per standardised unit in each trial. Exclusions kept , excluded_idx = exclude_trials ( pre , min_endpoint = 0.3 , max_endpoint = 1.5 , min_distance = 0.5 , max_distance = 4 , return_indices = True , ) Rows without a trajectory are never excluded. Thresholds you leave out are not applied. exclude_trials prints how many trials were excluded for each reason.

plot_binary_trials"] mmd --> use["average / select
downsample / save"] Module 1: preprocessing Input. A dataframe (or a list, one per participant) with one row per trial and the columns described in Input data . Extra rows (surveys, instructions) and extra columns are fine. What happens. Column check. check_columns looks for the needed columns under their usual names, or uses your column_map . A copy is added under the standard name ( response , accuracy , stimulus ...); your own columns are untouched. Row selection. Only rows that can be processed are filled in: they have mouse samples, a stimulus, button names and a screen size (and pass your optional row_mask ). The others are kept with empty new columns. Parsing. Button names, button rectangles and the start button are parsed; the image ID is extracted from the stimulus; the mouse samples become time , x and y arrays. Standardising. Pixels become standardised units: origin at the screen centre, one unit = half the shorter screen side ( scaling="min_side" , which keeps the aspect ratio), y pointing up. Button and start positions are converted the same way. Bookkeeping. ppt_number and repetition (how often a participant saw an image) are added if absent. Output. The same dataframe plus x_std , y_std , time , response_button_positions_std , starting_button_position_std , std_scale , repetition , ppt_number and the standard-named copies. processed_trial_mask(df) tells which rows hold a trajectory. Optional: exclusions. exclude_trials flags trials by endpoint and travelled distance and can return the excluded indices. Module 2: distance extraction Input. The preprocessed dataframe (optionally after exclusions). What happens. Trial selection. Rows with a trajectory are used. Participants, repetitions and images define the array's first three dimensions. Target order. For euclidean and cosine, the response buttons become the targets dimension, in the order you give with target_names (default: the order found in the data). Interpolation. Mouse samples are irregular. Each trial's x and y are linearly interpolated onto a regular grid ( sampling_interval , up to duration ). Before the first sample the array is NaN, unless fill_start=True places the cursor at the start button; after the last sample it is NaN. Metric. euclidean : distance to each button. cosine : cosine distance between the movement direction (from the start button) and each button's direction. position : x and y (or one of them) over time. Output. A MotorMovementData with named dimensions ( participants , repetitions , images , targets or coordinates , timepoints ), labels and metadata (metric, image IDs, button positions, start positions). From there: average , select , downsample , save .
